paragraphs: Stochastic bandit problems describe learning through repeated choices whose rewards are initially uncertain. This paper considers linear reward models in which the unknown parameter has a compact underlying structure. The central question is how much regret any learning algorithm must incur: how much reward it must lose, in the worst case, while discovering which choices are better.

The authors introduce a general definition of this structural compactness, called succinctness, and a framework for proving minimax regret lower bounds. Its organizing principle is an information–regret trade-off. Actions provide information about the unknown parameter, but acquiring that information can also cost reward. Lower bounds formalize the unavoidable cost of this learning process.

For vectors with only a few nonzero entries, the framework strengthens an existing lower bound. It also produces bounds for group-sparse parameters and low-rank matrices, which the authors describe as the first for those settings to their knowledge. These results help assess whether improved regret guarantees remain possible, rather than supplying a new bandit algorithm.
neurips-2025-a-novel-general-framework-f.tldr: A general information–regret framework establishes stronger or new limits on learning in bandits with compact parameter structures.

paragraphs: LLM rerankers improve retrieval results by reconsidering which documents best answer a query. Because processing long lists is expensive and context space is limited, systems commonly rank small groups and combine the results. Giving every query and group a fixed amount of computation overlooks an important difference: some relevance decisions are already clear, while others remain ambiguous.

AcuRank uses uncertainty to decide both how much additional reranking to perform and which documents deserve that attention. A Bayesian TrueSkill model maintains relevance estimates together with their uncertainty. These estimates are refined iteratively until confidence is sufficient, allowing the system to avoid repeatedly updating predictions it already considers confident.

On TREC-DL and BEIR, the authors report a consistently better balance between ranking accuracy and computational cost than fixed-computation baselines. They also find better scaling as more computation becomes available across different retrieval tasks and LLM rerankers. The practical contribution is an explicit mechanism for directing computation toward unresolved relevance decisions.
neurips-2025-acurank-uncertainty-aware-a.tldr: AcuRank directs reranking computation toward uncertain document relevance decisions, improving the measured accuracy–efficiency trade-off.

paragraphs: An adversarial example is an input modified to mislead a neural network. Some such examples also mislead other models, making their transferability an important property to study. This paper addresses the difficulty of transferring attacks between different architectures, including from convolutional networks to vision transformers, where existing enhancement methods still have limited success.

Spatial Adversarial Alignment fine-tunes the surrogate model used to construct attacks with guidance from a second, witness model. One component reduces differences between their features across both whole images and local regions. Another applies a self-adversarial strategy, using adversarial examples to impose additional constraints on how the models represent inputs.

Together, these components encourage the surrogate to concentrate on features shared with the witness model. Attacks directed at those features can then transfer more effectively. Experiments involving multiple architectures on ImageNet show increased transferability from aligned surrogates, especially across architecture families. The contribution is therefore a way to reshape the attack-generating model through feature alignment.
neurips-2025-boosting-adversarial-transf.tldr: Aligning a surrogate model’s spatial and adversarial features with a witness model improves attack transferability, especially across architectures.

paragraphs: Temporal point processes model sequences of events occurring over time. Existing datasets largely emphasize a single kind of information, limiting evaluation of models that must connect event timing with language and visual context. DanmakuTPPBench addresses this gap using video comments whose meaning and timing can be considered alongside what appears on screen.

The benchmark has two complementary components. DanmakuTPP-Events draws on Bilibili bullet comments, pairing precise timestamps and comment text with corresponding video frames. DanmakuTPP-QA adds questions requiring reasoning across these temporal, textual, and visual elements. Its questions are constructed through a multi-agent pipeline using language models and multimodal language models.

The authors evaluate both classical temporal point process models and recent multimodal language models. Their results reveal substantial performance gaps and weaknesses in modeling events that involve multiple information types. By providing event data and a related reasoning task, the benchmark supports studying how temporal modeling and multimodal understanding can work together, with reported baselines establishing a starting point.
neurips-2025-danmakutppbench-a-multi-mod.tldr: DanmakuTPPBench combines video-comment events and question answering to test joint reasoning about timing, text, and visual content.

paragraphs: Understanding why an overparameterized network generalizes requires examining how training changes it over time. This paper studies large two-layer neural networks using dynamical mean field theory, a method from nonequilibrium statistical physics. The analysis focuses on a regime with large network width and a large number of training samples relative to input dimension.

In that regime, the authors show that different aspects of learning evolve on separated timescales. A slow timescale governs growth in Gaussian or Rademacher complexity, measures used to characterize the network’s capacity. They also establish a bias toward small complexity when the initialization itself has sufficiently small complexity, making the starting condition part of the result.

The timescale separation dynamically distinguishes feature learning from overfitting. At longer training times, the analysis identifies a feature-unlearning regime associated with non-monotonic test error. These findings describe how useful learning and later deterioration can arise at different stages of training within the studied model, rather than treating generalization as a property of network size alone.
neurips-2025-dynamical-decoupling-of-gen.tldr: A theoretical analysis separates feature learning and overfitting timescales in large two-layer networks under a specified large-sample regime.

paragraphs: Studies of language-model representations have found linear subspaces that distinguish true statements from false ones. This paper investigates how such a distinction might emerge through language modeling itself. The authors construct a transparent one-layer transformer that reproduces this behavior, providing a setting where the learning process can be examined directly.

The key ingredient is a particular pattern in the training distribution: factual statements occur alongside other factual statements, while false statements likewise occur together. Learning the distinction can therefore improve predictions of subsequent tokens. This supplies one concrete route by which truth-related structure becomes useful for the language-modeling objective. Experiments with pretrained models corroborate the co-occurrence pattern.

In the toy model, learning unfolds in two phases. The network quickly memorizes individual factual associations, then takes longer to develop a linear separation between true and false statements, further reducing its language-modeling loss. The result demonstrates a possible mechanism under this data setting; it does not establish that every truth representation must arise through the same process.
neurips-2025-emergence-of-linear-truth-e.tldr: A toy transformer shows how truth-related co-occurrence patterns can make linear truth representations emerge through next-token learning.

paragraphs: Different three-letter codons can encode the same amino acid, yet their usage can still influence translation efficiency and gene expression. Equi-mRNA builds these synonymous relationships directly into an mRNA language model. Its aim is to represent both the shared biological role of equivalent codons and the meaningful structure in how they are used.

The model expresses synonymous-codon symmetries through cyclic groups of two-dimensional rotations. It combines this mathematical prior with an auxiliary equivariance loss and symmetry-aware pooling. These mechanisms make codon relationships an explicit part of representation learning rather than relying only on an additional prediction objective to capture them.

The authors report accuracy improvements of up to approximately 10% on property-prediction tasks. Generated sequences are up to approximately four times more realistic under Fréchet BioDistance and preserve functional properties approximately 28% better than a vanilla baseline. Analysis of learned rotations also recovers known GC-content and tRNA-abundance patterns. Together, these findings connect the model’s structural design with measured predictive, generative, and interpretability benefits.
neurips-2025-equi-mrna-protein-translati.tldr: Equi-mRNA explicitly models synonymous-codon symmetries, improving reported mRNA prediction, generation, and biological interpretability.

paragraphs: Locating a named object in a 3D scene tests only part of spatial understanding. A description can also refer to an activity area, an empty space, or a small part of an object. Anywhere3D-Bench broadens evaluation to cover all four levels, asking models to connect referring expressions with three-dimensional bounding boxes.

The benchmark contains 2,886 expression–box pairs. The authors test existing 3D grounding methods alongside language models and multimodal language models. Separating the grounding levels helps reveal different demands: identifying empty space requires reasoning about distances and spatial relationships, while identifying object parts requires detailed perception of how an object is composed.

The evaluation finds space-level and part-level grounding especially difficult. Even the strongest evaluated model, OpenAI o4-mini, reaches only 23.00% accuracy on spaces and 31.46% on parts, below its results for areas and whole objects. These findings show that success at locating objects can coexist with substantial weaknesses in understanding the surrounding space and internal object structure.
neurips-2025-from-objects-to-anywhere-a-.tldr: Anywhere3D-Bench reveals substantial weaknesses in locating empty spaces and object parts beyond standard whole-object grounding.

paragraphs: Electronic health records contain linked tables describing patient interactions and medical events over time. Privacy and regulatory constraints make sharing them difficult, motivating synthetic alternatives. Existing synthesis methods often reduce records to expert-selected features, such as a small set of vital signs or structured codes, narrowing the information represented in the generated data.

RawMed aims to synthesize records closer to their raw, multi-table form. It uses text-based representations and compression to capture complex relationships and temporal behavior with minimal lossy preprocessing. The central contribution is preserving more of the database’s organization and sequence structure instead of defining the synthesis task around a small, manually chosen feature set.

The paper also introduces an evaluation framework covering distributional similarity, relationships between tables, temporal dynamics, and privacy. On two open-source EHR datasets, RawMed outperforms baseline models in fidelity and utility. These results support evaluating synthetic records as connected histories across tables, with usefulness depending on more than whether individual variables resemble their real counterparts.
neurips-2025-generating-multi-table-time.tldr: RawMed generates linked, time-varying synthetic health records with minimal lossy preprocessing and improves measured fidelity and utility.

paragraphs: During ordinary autoregressive generation, a language model predicts probabilities for possible next tokens, selects one, and feeds only that selection back into the model. The probability distribution is discarded. Mixture of Inputs asks whether keeping some of that richer information can improve subsequent generation without changing the model through additional training.

The method still generates a discrete token in the standard way. It then forms a continuous input using Bayesian estimation: the predicted distribution serves as a prior, and the selected token serves as the observation. The resulting posterior expectation replaces the usual one-hot input, blending information about the chosen token with information about the other possibilities.

This changes what the model receives at the next step while preserving discrete text generation. The authors report consistently improved performance across several models on mathematical reasoning, code generation, and PhD-level question answering, together with improved text quality and reasoning. They describe the computational overhead as negligible. The findings support retaining distributional information as a practical, training-free generation modification.
neurips-2025-mixture-of-inputs-text-gene.tldr: Mixture of Inputs improves generation without training by feeding back a Bayesian blend of the sampled token and its predicted distribution.

paragraphs: Molecular analysis draws on knowledge spanning chemistry and biology. Although molecular language models can transfer across tasks, the authors identify limited knowledge and reasoning as obstacles to accurately explaining molecular features. Mol-LLaMA is designed to support broader molecular understanding, combining feature comprehension with informative explanations and reasoning.

The approach addresses both the data used to develop these abilities and the representations supplied to the model. The authors design key data types around fundamental molecular features and abilities needed for molecular reasoning. They also introduce a module that combines complementary information from different molecular encoders, drawing on the distinct strengths of their representations.

Experiments indicate that Mol-LLaMA can understand general molecular features and produce informative responses. These findings suggest potential as a general-purpose molecular analysis assistant. The significance lies in bringing knowledge-oriented data design together with multiple molecular representations, so that the model’s responses can reflect a broader understanding of molecules rather than relying on a single representation alone.
neurips-2025-mol-llama-towards-general-u.tldr: Mol-LLaMA combines molecular reasoning data and complementary encoders to support informative explanations of molecular features.

paragraphs: Language models can handle many tasks through prompting, but specialized applications often still benefit from fine-tuning. Obtaining enough domain-specific training examples can be difficult. A common response is to ask an LLM to generate more examples from a small seed collection, yet that collection can constrain both the diversity and quality of the resulting synthetic data.

PANGEA starts by identifying these limitations, especially when only a handful of domain examples are available. It then uses large amounts of publicly available general-purpose data to support synthetic-data generation. Crucially, this source material can be entirely unrelated to the target domain, expanding the material available beyond the small domain-specific collection.

The authors report that this approach produces more diverse, higher-quality synthetic data and validate its effectiveness on GSM8K, MedQA, FinQA, and a custom domain-specific language task. The practical insight is that unrelated data can still contribute to domain adaptation through the generation process. This broadens the resources that can support fine-tuning when specialized examples are scarce.
neurips-2025-pangea-projection-based-aug.tldr: PANGEA uses unrelated general-purpose data to improve the diversity and quality of synthetic examples for domain adaptation.

paragraphs: Moving a SQL query between database systems requires preserving its meaning while adapting system-specific functions, data types, and syntax. This differs from generating SQL from a natural-language request. PARROT targets this translation problem, which existing SQL benchmarks poorly capture because they cover too few systems and too little dialect-specific behavior.

The core benchmark contains 598 translation pairs drawn from 38 open-source benchmarks and real-world business services. These pairs are prepared to challenge understanding of database-specific SQL. Two additional variants serve different evaluation needs: PARROT-Diverse provides 28,003 translations for broad syntax testing, while PARROT-Simple supplies 5,306 representative samples for focused stress testing.

The benchmark variants cover 22 production-grade database systems. Reported LLM results average below 38.53% accuracy, indicating that translating between SQL dialects remains difficult in this evaluation. By making system differences central to the task, PARROT provides a way to assess a practical capability that success on conventional text-to-SQL benchmarks may not adequately establish.
neurips-2025-parrot-a-benchmark-for-eval.tldr: PARROT tests SQL translation across database systems and exposes substantial difficulty with dialect-specific functions, types, and syntax.

paragraphs: A world model lets an agent anticipate how its environment will behave. Deep-learning approaches can require substantial training data and struggle to update flexibly from sparse observations. Representing a world model as source code offers another route, but previous applications of program-structured models have largely focused on natural-language and grid-world settings.

PoE-World extends this approach to more complex environments by combining programmatic experts synthesized by language models. It represents the world through an exponentially weighted product of these experts. This composition provides a way to build a model from multiple program components while accommodating stochastic behavior rather than requiring a purely deterministic environment.

The authors show that the method can learn complex world models from a few observations. They evaluate those models inside a model-based planning agent on Atari’s Pong and Montezuma’s Revenge, reporting efficient performance and generalization to unseen levels. These results demonstrate the potential of compositional program representations for planning beyond the simpler domains previously associated with program-structured world modeling.
neurips-2025-poe-world-compositional-wor.tldr: PoE-World combines LLM-generated programmatic experts to learn stochastic world models from few observations and support planning.

paragraphs: Neural representations can encode sensitive or unwanted concepts alongside information needed for a useful task. Removing those concepts after training can therefore damage the task’s signal. SPLINCE addresses this tension by requiring concept removal to preserve a specific relationship: the covariance between the transformed representation and the target label.

The method uses an oblique projection to remove unwanted directions while protecting those label correlations. The authors establish it as the unique solution that eliminates linear predictability of the concept, maintains target covariance, and minimizes embedding distortion. The guarantee is specifically about linear concept predictability and covariance, making the preserved quantity mathematically explicit.

On benchmarks including Bias in Bios and Winobias, SPLINCE outperforms baselines at removing protected attributes while causing little damage to main-task information. The contribution connects a precise preservation criterion with an empirical benefit: representations can be altered to reduce unwanted linear signals while retaining the label relationships covered by the method. This gives concept removal a more targeted objective than simply suppressing sensitive directions.
neurips-2025-preserving-task-relevant-in.tldr: SPLINCE removes linear concept predictability while exactly preserving target-label covariance and minimizing representation distortion.

paragraphs: Process reward models evaluate intermediate reasoning rather than only the eventual answer. Existing versions often learn from final output responses and struggle with traces that contain a separate thinking trajectory followed by a response. ReasonFlux-PRM is designed around this trajectory–response structure, using supervision at both individual-step and whole-trajectory levels.

The resulting rewards support three uses across training and inference. They can select reasoning examples for distilling a larger model into a smaller one, provide dense feedback during reinforcement learning, and guide selection among multiple answers at test time. These uses connect the evaluation of a reasoning process with concrete decisions about data, policy updates, and final responses.

On benchmarks including AIME, MATH500, and GPQA-Diamond, the authors report that the 7B model selects better data than strong process reward models and human-curated baselines. Reported average gains are 12.1% for supervised fine-tuning, 4.5% for reinforcement learning, and 6.3% for test-time scaling. A 1.5B version is also released for more constrained applications.
neurips-2025-reasonflux-prm-trajectory-a.tldr: ReasonFlux-PRM evaluates reasoning steps and complete trajectories to improve data selection, reinforcement learning, and test-time answer selection.

paragraphs: Gossip algorithms allow a network to compute collectively using only communication between neighbors. This decentralized structure is useful when communication is constrained, but ordinary mean estimation is vulnerable to extreme values from corrupted or malicious nodes. The paper develops a route to an outlier-resistant estimate without requiring centralized communication.

The first component, GoRank, estimates global ranks through gossip. The second, GoTrim, uses rank estimation to compute a trimmed mean, a statistic that reduces the influence of extreme observations. The key connection is that local exchanges can build the global ordering information needed for a robust aggregate across an arbitrary communication graph.

The authors prove convergence rates of order 1/t for both rank estimation and trimmed-mean estimation, where t counts iterations. They also analyze GoTrim’s breakdown point, addressing its tolerance to contamination. Experiments spanning different network topologies, data distributions, and contamination schemes support the theoretical results. Together, the methods extend decentralized aggregation beyond a mean that is easily distorted by outliers.
neurips-2025-robust-distributed-estimati.tldr: GoRank and GoTrim enable decentralized rank and robust mean estimation with proven 1/t convergence rates.

paragraphs: Preference-based alignment typically trains on a fixed dataset, but real users’ preferences vary across populations, language patterns, and cultural contexts. A model aligned to one preference distribution may perform poorly when that distribution changes. This paper treats such shifts as an explicit optimization problem rather than assuming the training preferences remain representative.

The authors develop two distributionally robust versions of direct preference optimization: Wasserstein DPO and Kullback–Leibler DPO. Both use a robust optimization framework to address preference uncertainty. Their challenging minimax objectives are approximated to obtain scalable learning algorithms that use gradient-descent-style updates, connecting the robust formulation with a practical training procedure.

The paper also characterizes sample complexity for learning optimal policy parameters under each method. Experiments with benchmark datasets and language models report substantially improved alignment when preference distributions shift. The contribution therefore combines a formal treatment of learning under preference variation with computational methods and empirical evidence, focused on the mismatch between static training preferences and changing deployment conditions.
neurips-2025-robust-llm-alignment-via-di.tldr: Two distributionally robust DPO methods improve reported alignment under shifts between training and deployment preferences.

paragraphs: Neural spike trains record when neurons fire, and Poisson generalized linear models are widely used to analyze them. Standard implementations group spike times into count bins, which limits temporal resolution and scalability. This paper develops methods for the continuous-time counterpart, aiming to retain precise timing while making large recordings more tractable.

The authors introduce stochastic optimization methods and polynomial approximations for these models. They also use exponentially scaled Laguerre polynomials as an orthogonal temporal basis. This choice improves identification of temporal filters and, under the polynomial approximation, allows the relevant integrals to be evaluated in closed form, helping address the computational demands of continuous-time modeling.

Tests on synthetic data and real rodent hippocampal recordings show better accuracy and scalability than traditional binned GLMs. The resulting functional-connectivity estimates operate at temporal precision on the order of synaptic dynamics. GPU-optimized, open-source implementations of both estimators support adoption. The advance combines a more temporally precise model with computational techniques that make it practical for larger neural datasets.
neurips-2025-scalable-inference-of-funct.tldr: Continuous-time GLM estimators improve the accuracy and scalability of functional connectivity inference while preserving fine spike timing.

paragraphs: A detector trained on one video generator may struggle with another if it relies on conspicuous content mistakes specific to its training source. This paper instead directs attention toward low-level traces introduced by generative architectures. The authors first study different architectures to identify discriminative features shared across models and robust to impairments.

They then introduce an augmentation strategy based on wavelet decomposition, which separates information into frequency-related bands. Replacing selected bands during training encourages the detector to use more relevant forensic cues. The method aims to improve generalization without complex algorithms or a large training collection covering many different synthetic generators.

The evaluation trains a detector on videos from a single generator and tests it on outputs from a wide range of other models. The authors report a significant accuracy improvement over state-of-the-art detectors, including strong results on NOVA and FLUX. These findings support shaping what a detector learns through targeted augmentation, so that training on one generator can transfer more effectively to others.
neurips-2025-seeing-what-matters-general.tldr: Wavelet-based training augmentation helps synthetic-video detectors learn forensic cues that transfer across generators.

paragraphs: Evaluating an open-ended language-model response often means comparing its meaning with a reference answer. Similarity measures can instead respond to shared wording or sentence structure. Existing evaluation datasets also face costly human annotation, limited domain coverage, and ambiguous definitions of equivalence, making semantic evaluation itself difficult to assess.

Semantic-KG uses knowledge graphs to construct natural-language statement pairs with similar or different meanings. Dissimilar pairs are divided into four types of semantic variation. This structured generation method produces benchmarks in general knowledge, biomedicine, finance, and biology, allowing evaluation to examine both the kind of meaning change and the subject area.

The authors compare traditional language-processing scores with judgments made by LLMs. Performance depends on both domain and semantic-variation type, and no method is consistently best. These findings make the benchmark useful for diagnosing where a similarity measure succeeds or fails. They also show why an LLM judge’s ability to detect meaning should be assessed across different semantic changes and domains.
neurips-2025-semantic-kg-using-knowledge.tldr: Semantic-KG generates structured meaning-comparison benchmarks and finds that similarity methods vary substantially across domains and semantic changes.

paragraphs: Time-series classifiers often depend on meaningful short patterns, called shapelets. Yet many methods for explaining their predictions assign importance to individual timesteps. ShapeX builds explanations around subsequences instead, following the premise that the patterns driving a decision are often more meaningful as complete units than as isolated points.

Its Shapelet Describe-and-Detect framework learns a diverse collection of shapelets important for classification. ShapeX uses these to divide a series into meaningful segments, then applies Shapley values to assess each segment’s contribution. This connects the units used in an explanation with the types of patterns that the paper identifies as central to classification.

The authors further demonstrate causal relationships in the resulting explanations, attributing this property to the atomicity of shapelets. On synthetic and real-world datasets, ShapeX outperforms existing methods in finding the most relevant subsequences, improving precision and causal fidelity. The result supports treating meaningful temporal patterns as the explanatory units when analyzing how a time-series model reaches its decisions.
neurips-2025-shapex-shapelet-driven-post.tldr: ShapeX explains time-series predictions through shapelet-based segments, improving identification of relevant subsequences and reported causal fidelity.

paragraphs: Zero-shot vision-and-language navigation asks an agent to follow instructions through an unfamiliar 3D environment without scene-specific training. Over a long route, actions must remain consistent with both the physical layout and the instruction’s intent. STRIDER addresses failures caused by weak decision structure and insufficient use of feedback from earlier actions.

The framework combines two mechanisms. A Structured Waypoint Generator uses spatial layout information to constrain the available actions. A Task-Alignment Regulator adjusts behavior according to progress through the task. Together, these components organize where the agent can go and use execution feedback to keep its choices connected to what the instruction requires.

Experiments on R2R-CE and RxR-CE show improvements over strong state-of-the-art methods across key metrics. The abstract highlights a success-rate increase from 29% to 35%, a relative gain of 20.7%. These results support the value of combining spatially structured decisions with progress-sensitive feedback for navigating unseen environments, rather than relying on each action decision in isolation.
neurips-2025-strider-navigation-via-inst.tldr: STRIDER combines spatially constrained waypoints and task-progress feedback to improve zero-shot navigation in unseen 3D environments.

paragraphs: Reasoning models can generate responses that are longer than a problem warrants, increasing inference cost. DIET incorporates estimated problem difficulty into reinforcement learning so that pressure to shorten a response depends on the task. It adjusts both token penalties and target lengths as difficulty is estimated during training.

Implementing this objective requires care in group-normalized reinforcement learning methods such as GRPO. The authors analyze problems with naively weighting rewards and introduce Advantage Weighting to apply the difficulty-aware objectives stably and effectively. The training design therefore addresses both what response lengths should depend on and how that preference enters the learning procedure.

Experiments show reduced token counts alongside improved reasoning performance. Shorter, high-quality samples also improve majority-vote inference scaling under fixed computational budgets. In addition, DIET strengthens the positive relationship between problem difficulty and response length, allocating more verbosity to harder tasks. These findings make efficiency a question of distributing reasoning effort appropriately, with benefits extending beyond reducing the length of a single answer.
neurips-2025-the-overthinker-s-diet-cutt.tldr: DIET adapts response-length penalties to problem difficulty, reducing tokens while improving reported reasoning and fixed-budget inference scaling.

paragraphs: Machine unlearning aims to remove selected data’s influence without retraining a model from scratch. Existing guarantees can compare an unlearned model statistically with a retrained one, but they do not naturally extend to outputs on adversarially perturbed inputs. This paper examines what happens near the examples the model was supposed to forget.

The authors identify cases where a slightly changed forget sample is recognized by the unlearned model even though the retrained model fails to recognize it. They formalize this persistence as residual knowledge and show that it is inevitable in high-dimensional settings. The concern is that information may remain accessible in a sample’s local neighborhood despite apparent forgetting.

To address it, the paper proposes RURK, a fine-tuning strategy that penalizes recognition of perturbed forget samples. Experiments with deep networks on vision benchmarks find residual knowledge across existing unlearning methods and show that RURK effectively prevents it in those evaluations. The work expands the target of unlearning from behavior on original samples to behavior on nearby perturbed versions.
neurips-2025-the-unseen-threat-residual-.tldr: Perturbed forgotten samples can expose residual knowledge after unlearning; RURK targets this vulnerability through fine-tuning.
